   PLEASE SEND YOUR TEXTFILE!
Text is accepted in any form for
OUTLETTERS: wordprocessor files
(say which),typed or handwritten
letters. However, PLEASE send us
a textfile if possible so your
letter needn't be typed again!
The easiest for us to edit are
Tasword 2 files with the right
margin set at 32 but a textfile
in ANY format is appreciated!

Please state if there should be
parts of your letter you do not
wish published but we always use
our discretion anyway. Letters
may also be edited for clarity
and length... Please ask if you
welcome direct correspondence
from other OUTLET readers and we
will publish your full address.

From Miles Kinloch, EDINBURGH

Dear Brian,

The hi-byte part of system vari-
able 23668/9 could be used as a
very easy way of telling which
mode a Spectrum was in. It would
not be fooled either like some
tests can be by POKE 23611,205
(i.e. to allow graphics T and U
to be printed).

The difference is due to the
command syntax table being at a
different place in the 128K ROM.
Although the lo-byte changes
with the command being used, the
hi-byte should always stay the
same in a given mode. Try this,
for instance:-


  10 IF PEEK 23669=26 THEN PRINT
    "You're in 48K mode":GOTO 30
  20 PRINT "You are in 128K
     mode": REM (regardless of
     machine)
  30 STOP

Ironically, the Speccy manual
describes this sys var as "very
unlikely to be useful"!


Here's another quick tip. If
anyone with a +D ever gets a
program written for the OPUS
DISCOVERY, here's how to make
the +D recognise the OPUS forms
of LOAD and SAVE, so that such a
program could then be run with-
out needing to change the syntax
first.


The following POKEs will alter
the Microdrive syntax to the
OPUS forms LOAD *1;"file" etc.
These POKEs should therefore be
regarded as temporary, to be
used only if and when required,
rather than incorporated perm-
anently into the DOS, because
the normal Microdrive syntax is
disabled as a result. Anyway,
here are the POKEs - only 4 are
needed:-
  POKE @1712,0: POKE @1713,0:
  POKE @1714,0: POKE @1735,10

Now all the OPUS forms of LOAD,
SAVE, VERIFY and MERGE commands
should work, (but not OPEN #,
MOVE, FORMAT etc. - the OPUS
handles these quite differently
from the +D.)
                  Miles Kinloch

Brian Cavers to Miles Kinloch

Many thanks, Miles. That 48/128K
test is just what we want and it
really looks foolproof. Since
the syntax table MUST be differ-
ent in 128K mode then it is hard
to see how it can fail and we
shall adopt it in OUTLET. What
with this and Malcolm Goodman's
super TOGGLER switch we now have
more chance of coping with those
difficult programs where the
mode either needs detecting or
changing or both!

All your other DOS info will be
compiled into an article in a
future OUTLET along with the
programs.
                     Brian

From Malcolm Perry,KIDDERMINSTER

I have just been reading Chris
Ingram's letter outlining his
problems [OUTLETTERS 82]. In one
respect the crashes do seem to
duplicate the problems I have
experienced in the past. Some of
my points most likely duplicate
those made by Brian in his
reply.

Firstly, his problem goes away
after a time from first switch
on. This reflects what I get due
to dirty edge connectors. I find
I need to give mine a clean
about every 6 months. I have
tried various cleaners but
beware of some of the switch
cleaners as they melt plastic!


I find methalated spirit as good
as anything.I soak a cotton bud,
the things with a blob of cotton
wool on each end of a stick,with
the meths and give the Spectrum
connector a good rub. Then, with
it still wet, plug the Disciple
on and off a couple of times.

[IT GOES WITHOUT SAYING BUT IT'S
SO IMPORTANT: ALWAYS HAVE EVERY-
THING SWITCHED OFF IF CONNECTING
AND DISCONNECTING - OR EVEN JUST
"FIDDLING" WITH ANYTHING PLUGGED
IN THE EDGE CONNECTOR! - Ed]

It is then usually OK for the
next six months. The slight oily
film left by some switch clean-
ers seems to give more trouble
than the dry surface from meths.


Secondly, Chris found things got
worse with time;it starts off OK
then puts up odd characters or
coloured blocks on screen and
eventually crashes and locks up.
That is how one of mine that had
one or more faulty RAM ICs be-
haved. This is proved by blowing
cold air through vents (hair
dryer on cold) because normal
operation is then restored.

Using a ribbon cable between a
Disciple and computer can cause
problems. Mine totally refuses
to work even with just a few
inches of cable yet the +D is OK
with the same cable. Also, the
Disciple refuses to work with a
128 if a solid "T" adaptor is
used yet is OK with the adaptor
and a 48k!

The system with a Disciple even
refuses to work if the solid "T"
adaptor is used on the back of
the Disciple with the Disciple
directly on the computer!

The Disciple with a +2 I find is
a problem as there is no provis-
ion to fix it as with a 48/128.
It has a tendency to move about
more and thus crash.

To prove if the problem is due
to a faulty computer or an
external dirty mains supply, try
using it on its own with a
simple routine and let it run
for an hour or so. This should
show if the computer crashes.
now and again give it a tap or
slight move to simulate actual
use.

If it survives this test then
try it at an elevated tempera-
ture.In fact this is recommended
in the official repair manual.
With it running, raise the
temperature using a hair drier.

 [Not close enough for heat but
 only for slight warmth! Do this
 at your own risk! - Ed]


This test is normally done with
the computer open and the ICs
warmed up, otherwise blow the
warm air through the vents. This
shows if one or more ICs are
faulty, However, such a test
could fail any suspect ICs
permanently or, if too hot, fail
good components - so be warned!


This sort of test duplicates the
extra heat introduced by such as
a Disciple being fitted.

I suffered a lot of crashes due
to the 'fridge, kettle, lights,
and so on around the house
although the actual mains is
quite stable in this area. I now
have extensive filters,suppress-
ors and mains spike"clippers" in
the mains to the computer equip-
ment and have little problem
now.

POKE @11. This VAR. has a pecul-
iarity. If set on BOOT so that
the +D uses its own printer port
it overwrites the print routine
in the Spectrum with its own
code.


If set on BOOT to use the Spec-
trum printer then it leaves the
Spectrum routine intact. There-
fore it can subsequently be
poked with "0" to cause the +D
to modify the print routine to
use its own port.

Booting with it set to "0" how-
ever, directly overwrites the
Spectrum routine but doing a
subsequent poke "1" cannot
restore the original routine.

You need to poke the VAR with
"1", resave DOS, reset Spectrum
then reboot to be able to change
from +D printer to Spectrum
printer. The handbook indication
that it can be "turned on and
off" is a bit misleading.


My Disciple and +D behave as
described. I am not aware of a
"fix". However, as I use data
buffers between computer and
printer the Spectrum can perform
an LPRINT irrespective of the
state of the printer.

The difference between the +D
and Disciple in the way it
responds to not having a printer
connected at all is down to a
hardware difference.The Disciple
requires both logic HIGH (busy)
and LOW (ready) signals from the
printer to determine if data can
be sent.If there is no signal at
all (ie no printer) it defaults
to "send data" condition. (I
presume all Disciples are the
same).


The +D only requires one logic
level from the printer (low) to
tell it to send data. OFF LINE
and NO PRINTER are to the +D the
same and a condition that it is
not to send data.

Both these arrangements have
their advantages and disadvant-
ages.

It is possible to add say a push
button to the +D that, when
pressed, brings the appropriate
control line to the correct
logic level when no printer is
connected. This would fool the
+D into thinking a printer is on
line so letting it execute the
LPRINT instruction (obviously
the print data is lost).


Another possibility is to design
a "logic box" between computer
and printer that will detect if
there is no printer and so pro-
vide the appropriate control to
the +D so that it behaves like
the Disciple - if "no printer"
is a real problem.

While on the subject of printers
it may be of interest that dev-
ices are available to match ser-
ial output to parallel printers
or parallel output to serial.

Checking data leads by visible
inspection (even with a magnify-
ing glass) may not show up a
problem: while the lead may seem
to be firmly held in the connec-
tor it may not be making a prop-
er connection.

When you consider the somewhat
"crude" method in that it relies
in the connector contact cutting
through the ribbon cable insul-
ation onto the conductors as the
halves are pressed together. A
continuity test between each end
connector on every pin while
moving the cable at its ends may
be long-winded but necessary to
show up a problem.

Disc drive PSUs are a subject in
their own right. First,there are
two main types: those requiring
12V and 5V. However, later types
only require 5V. Different ones
I have had dealings with vary in
their current requirements but
in general can take up to 500mA,
the stepper motor being the most
current-demanding.

Just a thought,what is the mains
voltage in Malawi? The PSUs from
here are probably designed for
240V. Is the voltage standard
there 220V? Even if the PSU is
marked 220/240V it could well be
it is only just sufficiently
rated to work in this country at
240V.This could well explain why
a 350mA PSU failed to work over
there but is OK here. It's not
so much the current rating as
the voltage rating. I had prob-
lems with an MGT drive with a
built-in PSU.Although the trans-
former current rating was well
in excess of that required, its
voltage rating rating was too
low: it was only just sufficient
to work under good ideal condit-
ions.


Incidentally, measuring the
current taken by a drive can be
misleading due to the pulse
nature of the stepper motor. The
head needs to be moving to and
fro between T0 and T79 during
the test.


I fail to see why a PSU should
be declared as "unrepairable".
It might be uneconomical to
repair perhaps, because labour
charges far exceed the cost of a
new item. Unless it is a problem
say, with some odd type of comp-
onent or connector that cannot
now be obtained. After all a 5V,
stabilized PSU uses relatively
few components and these are
easily available (here any way).


A transformer, capacitor, and 5V
regulator is all my home made
drive PSUs consist of. I would
not recommend the normal plug in
PSUs available. They do need to
be well regulated and have good
smoothing (unless the drives are
of a type with the 5V regulator
in the drive housing itself and
the PSU is, therefore, unregul-
ated).


If a voltmeter is connected to
to the 5V supply at the drive
itself and the voltage is much
over 5.25V and/or falls below
4.75V with the drive running
(and the head moving across the
tracks) then suspect the PSU.



I am afraid none of this really
gives any specific answers but
may help to point in the right
direction.

                 Malcolm Perry

From W. Arnold Yates, LANCS.

Dear Chezron,

I have just bought a Discovery
twin disc drive and wonder if it
is possible to use a +D disk in
this drive or transfer programs
from one to the other, ie, +D to
Discovery and Discovery to +D.

I have the OUTLET Disc Extra 1
but the program for Discovery
won't work: all I get is B int-
eger out of range, 1000:1,1. I
have only just found this out
with not having an Opus Discov-
ery disk drive; I have never had
occasion to use it. Can you
please help me to get it to
work?
                     W.A. Yates

Brian Cavers to Arnold Yates

We do have software to read Opus
on +D and visa versa but it is
for double-density drives only
and we have had no success with
it at all.

You do not name the program on
Extra 1 but I guess you mean
TRANSBACK. I believe you have
the +D version of Extra 1 and
are loading TRANSBACK on your +D
system which gives the error you
report. TRANSBACK must be run on
your Opus system to save Opus
software to tape. You can then
use UNITRANS+ (OUTLET 20) on the
+D to load it from tape to +D
disk. To transfer TRANSBACK to
your Opus do the following...


1. You need a tape cassette
   recorder connected to the
   Spectrum using the +D. If
   you have a +2 then the one
   that is built in is fine
   but you will need another
   cassette machine attached
   to your Opus system.
2. If you have a 128K then
   switch to 48K mode.
3. Load TRANSBACK from +D.
4. Press BREAK.
5. Press R and the word RUN
   should appear.
6. Type 9983
7. Press ENTER and the prompt
   to save to tape should show.
8. Start the tape recording and
   press a key.
9. Load the program from the
   tape into your Opus system.


10.Ensure you have a disk with
   some room in your Opus drive.
10.Press BREAK on your Opus
   system.
11.Type RUN 9982.
12.Press ENTER
13.TRANSBACK should save to Opus
   disk.

You can now use TRANSBACK to get
software from Opus to tape and
then use UNITRANS+ on the +D to
get it from tape to +D disk.

                        Brian

From Peter Johnson,NEW ZEALAND



Dear Brian and Ron,

This my second letter since
joining. At the time of writing
I have received and attempted to
assimilate the contents of the
first few copies of OUTLET.


I am very impressed with the
range and variety of the
material presented.It must be a
difficult problem to maintain a
balance so that the various
interest areas are satisfied.
You seem to be able to achieve
this.


I was particularly interested in
the description of the extens-
ions to the SPECTRUM covered in
Issue 80 by Rick Schuitemaker
and also congratulate him on his
efforts.

I must admit that I had been
thinking along similar lines but
on a much more modest scale:that
of utilizing the unused capacity
of the 48K extension memory if
full-specification IC's are
used.

By way of explanation for new-
comers, when the SPECTRUM was
extended to 48K [from the orig-
inal 16K - Ed], the extra memory
IC's used were not full specifi-
cation types; they had some
defects.

The IC's were apparently sorted
into groups with useable upper
or lower sections, half the IC
was still functional and fitted
to the Spectrum. There is a wire
link on the circuit board to
select which group of IC's were
used.

If full specification IC's are
used there is a further 32K of
memory available. To use this
requires some additional hard-
ware in the form of two or three
extra IC's to be fitted some-
where to do the switching as
with other larger memory vers-
ions of the SPECTRUM. It is so
obvious that I am sure that this
must have been done before but I
have seen nothing published.)


Back to the extensions by Rick:
I am interested in doing this
extension work to at least one
of my 48K Spectrums. Although I
have the facilities to design
and produce the circuit boards
there is no point in duplicating
the effort if boards are avail-
able.


In addition, mention was made of
extra ROMs containing the
additional functions to make use
of the extensions. May I ask
through these letters if the
ROMs and circuit board are, or
could be made,available? The ROM
is most essential to fully
explore the potential of this
development.


I make no secret that my inter-
est is in the more technical
area and I would expect some
criticism that the emphasis
could be shifting in the content
of OUTLET.My opinion is that the
two interests are complimentry:
without hardware there would be
no need for software and visa
versa.For the SPECTRUM to conti-
nue it is necessary for it to be
further developed and extended;
its good features enhanced and
it limitations minimised.

I have started to prepare a"wish
list" of items where I think
further development can be done.
This I may forward to OUTLET in
due course. I can contribute to
the hardware side but am still a
learner in software.

If we all attempt to understand
something of what is published,
be it in software or hardware,
there is a further advance in
our understanding of the Spec-
trum.

In my original letter published
in OUTLET 81, I mentioned my
other interest in amateur radio
and that I used a Spectrum as a
terminal for the amateur radio
packet system (as a reminder,
packet radio is a worldwide
system of linked bulletin boards
using radio). What I did not
mention was that I can be
contacted by this means at
address ZL4LV @ ZL4AA. ZL4lV is
my amateur radio call sign and
ZL4AA is the local bulletin
board call sign.

The ZL stands for New Zealand.
If any other OUTLET users use
this system I would be interest-
ed to hear from them. It should
also be possible to transmit
material for OUTLET by this
means.

                 Peter Johnson.

Brian Cavers to Peter Johnson

There is no need to be defensive
regarding topics of a technical
or hardware side of computing! I
for one am always delighted to
receive and publish such items
and am certain that many of our
readers are too. I would be more
than happy to have such articles
in every single issue - to some
extent that is what DRIVECHAT is
intended to be, though it covers
a wider miscellany of material.

I have been snowed under these
last months, what with rewriting
routines in the PC version and
several days lost with 'flu but
I shall strive to prepare your
contributions for OUTLET soon!

Specifically regarding your idea
of gaining an extra 32K, that
method does ring a faint memory.
Way back in 1983, East London
Robotics used to supply 32K RAM
packs to upgrade a 16K Spectrum
to 48K. They also supplied a 64K
pack called SP80 which produced
an 80K Spectrum with two pages
of 32K which could be switched
in at 32768 to 65535. Included
with the RAM chips were three
control chips and an LED.

The commands: OUT 65407,0 and
OUT 49023,0 toggled between the
two 32K pages of memory and the
LED lit up for one but not the
other to indicate which was in
use. Of course, it was invisible
inside the case in normal use!


I do not know if the SP80 used
the same method you describe but
it is of interest.

I often wonder why some company
did not produce an extra 16K RAM
to page in over the ROM so games
could utilize the full 64K. Well
of course the answer is that RAM
was relatively expensive and it
would be pretty useless without
a significant number of games
being made available. Possibly
it might have been made useful
to the BASIC programmer with a
utility to copy the ROM into the
new RAM but with some tiny extra
routines overwritten unused or
little used areas.
                       Brian

Bill Clark, BARROW-IN-FURNESS

Dear Brian and Ron,

When using TYPELINER I can print
out using all kinds of different
print styles. Is it possible to
do this using TASWORD which is
what I'm using now. Also what is
DATA MERGE for and how do you
use it?

How do you alter TASWORD so that
you can print 80 characters per
line and print this out?

Do you know of any more secret
messages on the +3 apart from
the "HELLO, I'M A +3"? This also
works on the  +2 but gives the
same message as a +3.


I have an external +3 disk disk
drive. When plugged in the back
of my +3 I am given a report on
the option screen which says
Drives A: B: and M: available.

Unfortunately, all drives are
disabled and nothing works until
I disconnect my B: drive from
the computer. I have tried
various leads and different
power packs but to no success.

With the B: drive plugged in I
then go into +3 BASIC mode and
type LOAD "B:". Then I insert a
disk and type LOAD "filename".
Nothing happens. The disk motor
doesn't turn. It's as if the
computer doesn't know the drive
is there.


The same thing happens if I type
LOAD "A:". If Drive B: is
disconnected then the computer
recognizes Drive A:. If B: is
connected then the computer rec-
ognizes nothing.

Please try and solve this for me
as I've had all sorts of
problems and blew up 5 different
power packs which need repair-
ing.

         Best regards,


          Bill Clark

Brian Cavers to Bill Clark

You don't say which version of
Tasword you're using but I guess
it's Tasword +3.

Tasword +3 of itself can't print
out in different print styles.If
you have a printer with variable
fonts you can include printer
codes in your document in the
usual way, to change fonts and
get double-height/double width,
and so on if your printer has
these features.

Tasword produced a separate pro-
gram called TASPRINT PLUS THREE
with 25 different fonts and a
font designer, priced `24.95.It
works with Tasword documents.


Unfortunately, like all Spectrum
products,it is very difficult to
find any supplier these days. It
may be possible to get a copy at
a computer fair or why not put
in an advert in OUTBOARD or in
MICROMART for a secondhand copy?


DATA MERGE lets you include a
special character in your Tas-
word document (the ampersand &)
with a code letter. This acts as
a marker. When you print the
document using the "print with
Data merge" feature, as well as
the usual printer prompts, you
are asked to enter a filename.
As the document is printed the
marker is replaced with text
from this second file.


For example, you might have a
standard letter you repeatedly
send to people on request. You
might normally load the letter
into Tasword, type in the name
and address of the person and
any other details particular to
the case and then print it. If
instead you have a file full of
names and addresses flagged as a
data merge file you need only
type the marker in the letter.It
is obviously only of much use if
you are printing multiple copies
of a document.

The above example is known as
"mail-merge" but it can be any
text of course. In addition, you
can merge in MASTERFILE +3 data
saved with "data export".


Full details of DATA MERGE are
given in the Tasword +3 manual
starting at page 40.

To get 80 column...

1. Go to the main Tasword menu.
2. Press C to customise program.
3. Press ENTER to confirm.
4. Check TASWORD is in the drive
5. Press ENTER.
6. Press P to change the program
7. Press ENTER to confirm.
8. Press ENTER repeatedly until
   the flashing cursor goes down
   to "Right margin (64)"
9. Type 80.
10.Press ENTER repeatedly to end
11.Back at the custom menu.
12.Press EDIT for main menu.
13.Press R and ENTER for editor.


You should now be able to cursor
right and when you reach the
right side of the screen it will
scroll left so you can go beyond
64 columns,in fact, to a maximum
of 128 (even though 80 was put
in! Bug?).

When you reach column 80 set the
right margin in the usual way by
pressing EXTEND to get extended
mode then SYMBOL plus key "9"
(right bracket) together.


Note: to make this permanent I
think you need to resave TASWORD
using the T option at the main
menu. Otherwise, next time you
load the program it will default
to 64 columns again.


No, sorry, I don't know of any
other hidden features or mess-
ages of the +3 other than has
been listed in OUTLET over rec-
ent months. If you missed them
then scan back over OUTLETTERS
(see also John Garner's letter
in this issue).

It sounds like your B drive is
not connected right.Try MEEDMORE
DISTRIBUTION on 051 521 2202. I
believe they make up leads and
are said to be helpful. See also
James Castle's OUTLETTER with
the address of a supplier who
has "a lot of Sinclair leads".

If you have blown up five PSUs
then I can only guess the cable
to your B drive is shorting the
power.

Is it the PSU's in the B drive
that keep failing or the main
PSU to the +3?

If the cable is correctly wired
then surely you must have some
fault in the wiring of the B
drive or in the +3 B drive out-
put circuitry. Trouble is, I do
not know of any computer repair
company that will deal with +3
drive problems.

                          Brian

July, 1994        Page Reply

How to write to us...02     - Miles Kinloch........03    06 Malcolm Perry........07    15 W. Arnold Yates......22    23 James Castle.........26    27 Peter W. Johnson.....28    35 Bill Clark...........38    41 John Redfern.........48    51

PLEASE SEND YOUR TEXTFILE! Text is accepted in any form for OUTLETTERS: wordprocessor files (say which),typed or handwritten letters. However, PLEASE send us a textfile if possible so your letter needn't be typed again! The easiest for us to edit are Tasword 2 files with the right margin set at 32 but a textfile in ANY format is appreciated!

From Miles Kinloch, EDINBURGH

Dear Brian,

The hi-byte part of system vari- able 23668/9 could be used as a very easy way of telling which mode a Spectrum was in. It would not be fooled either like some tests can be by POKE 23611,205 (i.e. to allow graphics T and U to be printed).

The difference is due to the command syntax table being at a different place in the 128K ROM. Although the lo-byte changes with the command being used, the hi-byte should always stay the same in a given mode. Try this, for instance:-

10 IF PEEK 23669=26 THEN PRINT "You're in 48K mode":GOTO 30 20 PRINT "You are in 128K mode": REM (regardless of machine) 30 STOP

Ironically, the Speccy manual describes this sys var as "very unlikely to be useful"!

Here's another quick tip. If anyone with a +D ever gets a program written for the OPUS DISCOVERY, here's how to make the +D recognise the OPUS forms of LOAD and SAVE, so that such a program could then be run with- out needing to change the syntax first.

The following POKEs will alter the Microdrive syntax to the OPUS forms LOAD *1;"file" etc. These POKEs should therefore be regarded as temporary, to be used only if and when required, rather than incorporated perm- anently into the DOS, because the normal Microdrive syntax is disabled as a result. Anyway, here are the POKEs - only 4 are needed:- POKE @1712,0: POKE @1713,0: POKE @1714,0: POKE @1735,10

Now all the OPUS forms of LOAD, SAVE, VERIFY and MERGE commands should work, (but not OPEN #, MOVE, FORMAT etc. - the OPUS handles these quite differently from the +D.) Miles Kinloch

Brian Cavers to Miles Kinloch

Many thanks, Miles. That 48/128K test is just what we want and it really looks foolproof. Since the syntax table MUST be differ- ent in 128K mode then it is hard to see how it can fail and we shall adopt it in OUTLET. What with this and Malcolm Goodman's super TOGGLER switch we now have more chance of coping with those difficult programs where the mode either needs detecting or changing or both!

All your other DOS info will be compiled into an article in a future OUTLET along with the programs. Brian

From Malcolm Perry,KIDDERMINSTER

I have just been reading Chris Ingram's letter outlining his problems [OUTLETTERS 82]. In one respect the crashes do seem to duplicate the problems I have experienced in the past. Some of my points most likely duplicate those made by Brian in his reply.

Firstly, his problem goes away after a time from first switch on. This reflects what I get due to dirty edge connectors. I find I need to give mine a clean about every 6 months. I have tried various cleaners but beware of some of the switch cleaners as they melt plastic!

I find methalated spirit as good as anything.I soak a cotton bud, the things with a blob of cotton wool on each end of a stick,with the meths and give the Spectrum connector a good rub. Then, with it still wet, plug the Disciple on and off a couple of times.

[IT GOES WITHOUT SAYING BUT IT'S SO IMPORTANT: ALWAYS HAVE EVERY- THING SWITCHED OFF IF CONNECTING AND DISCONNECTING - OR EVEN JUST "FIDDLING" WITH ANYTHING PLUGGED IN THE EDGE CONNECTOR! - Ed]

It is then usually OK for the next six months. The slight oily film left by some switch clean- ers seems to give more trouble than the dry surface from meths.

Secondly, Chris found things got worse with time;it starts off OK then puts up odd characters or coloured blocks on screen and eventually crashes and locks up. That is how one of mine that had one or more faulty RAM ICs be- haved. This is proved by blowing cold air through vents (hair dryer on cold) because normal operation is then restored.

Using a ribbon cable between a Disciple and computer can cause problems. Mine totally refuses to work even with just a few inches of cable yet the +D is OK with the same cable. Also, the Disciple refuses to work with a 128 if a solid "T" adaptor is used yet is OK with the adaptor and a 48k!

The system with a Disciple even refuses to work if the solid "T" adaptor is used on the back of the Disciple with the Disciple directly on the computer!

The Disciple with a +2 I find is a problem as there is no provis- ion to fix it as with a 48/128. It has a tendency to move about more and thus crash.

To prove if the problem is due to a faulty computer or an external dirty mains supply, try using it on its own with a simple routine and let it run for an hour or so. This should show if the computer crashes. now and again give it a tap or slight move to simulate actual use.

If it survives this test then try it at an elevated tempera- ture.In fact this is recommended in the official repair manual. With it running, raise the temperature using a hair drier.

[Not close enough for heat but only for slight warmth! Do this at your own risk! - Ed]

This test is normally done with the computer open and the ICs warmed up, otherwise blow the warm air through the vents. This shows if one or more ICs are faulty, However, such a test could fail any suspect ICs permanently or, if too hot, fail good components - so be warned!

This sort of test duplicates the extra heat introduced by such as a Disciple being fitted.

I suffered a lot of crashes due to the 'fridge, kettle, lights, and so on around the house although the actual mains is quite stable in this area. I now have extensive filters,suppress- ors and mains spike"clippers" in the mains to the computer equip- ment and have little problem now.

POKE @11. This VAR. has a pecul- iarity. If set on BOOT so that the +D uses its own printer port it overwrites the print routine in the Spectrum with its own code.

If set on BOOT to use the Spec- trum printer then it leaves the Spectrum routine intact. There- fore it can subsequently be poked with "0" to cause the +D to modify the print routine to use its own port.

Booting with it set to "0" how- ever, directly overwrites the Spectrum routine but doing a subsequent poke "1" cannot restore the original routine.

You need to poke the VAR with "1", resave DOS, reset Spectrum then reboot to be able to change from +D printer to Spectrum printer. The handbook indication that it can be "turned on and off" is a bit misleading.

My Disciple and +D behave as described. I am not aware of a "fix". However, as I use data buffers between computer and printer the Spectrum can perform an LPRINT irrespective of the state of the printer.

The difference between the +D and Disciple in the way it responds to not having a printer connected at all is down to a hardware difference.The Disciple requires both logic HIGH (busy) and LOW (ready) signals from the printer to determine if data can be sent.If there is no signal at all (ie no printer) it defaults to "send data" condition. (I presume all Disciples are the same).

The +D only requires one logic level from the printer (low) to tell it to send data. OFF LINE and NO PRINTER are to the +D the same and a condition that it is not to send data.

Both these arrangements have their advantages and disadvant- ages.

It is possible to add say a push button to the +D that, when pressed, brings the appropriate control line to the correct logic level when no printer is connected. This would fool the +D into thinking a printer is on line so letting it execute the LPRINT instruction (obviously the print data is lost).

Another possibility is to design a "logic box" between computer and printer that will detect if there is no printer and so pro- vide the appropriate control to the +D so that it behaves like the Disciple - if "no printer" is a real problem.

While on the subject of printers it may be of interest that dev- ices are available to match ser- ial output to parallel printers or parallel output to serial.

Checking data leads by visible inspection (even with a magnify- ing glass) may not show up a problem: while the lead may seem to be firmly held in the connec- tor it may not be making a prop- er connection.

When you consider the somewhat "crude" method in that it relies in the connector contact cutting through the ribbon cable insul- ation onto the conductors as the halves are pressed together. A continuity test between each end connector on every pin while moving the cable at its ends may be long-winded but necessary to show up a problem.

Disc drive PSUs are a subject in their own right. First,there are two main types: those requiring 12V and 5V. However, later types only require 5V. Different ones I have had dealings with vary in their current requirements but in general can take up to 500mA, the stepper motor being the most current-demanding.

Just a thought,what is the mains voltage in Malawi? The PSUs from here are probably designed for 240V. Is the voltage standard there 220V? Even if the PSU is marked 220/240V it could well be it is only just sufficiently rated to work in this country at 240V.This could well explain why a 350mA PSU failed to work over there but is OK here. It's not so much the current rating as the voltage rating. I had prob- lems with an MGT drive with a built-in PSU.Although the trans- former current rating was well in excess of that required, its voltage rating rating was too low: it was only just sufficient to work under good ideal condit- ions.

Incidentally, measuring the current taken by a drive can be misleading due to the pulse nature of the stepper motor. The head needs to be moving to and fro between T0 and T79 during the test.

I fail to see why a PSU should be declared as "unrepairable". It might be uneconomical to repair perhaps, because labour charges far exceed the cost of a new item. Unless it is a problem say, with some odd type of comp- onent or connector that cannot now be obtained. After all a 5V, stabilized PSU uses relatively few components and these are easily available (here any way).

A transformer, capacitor, and 5V regulator is all my home made drive PSUs consist of. I would not recommend the normal plug in PSUs available. They do need to be well regulated and have good smoothing (unless the drives are of a type with the 5V regulator in the drive housing itself and the PSU is, therefore, unregul- ated).

If a voltmeter is connected to to the 5V supply at the drive itself and the voltage is much over 5.25V and/or falls below 4.75V with the drive running (and the head moving across the tracks) then suspect the PSU.

I am afraid none of this really gives any specific answers but may help to point in the right direction.

Malcolm Perry

From W. Arnold Yates, LANCS.

Dear Chezron,

I have just bought a Discovery twin disc drive and wonder if it is possible to use a +D disk in this drive or transfer programs from one to the other, ie, +D to Discovery and Discovery to +D.

I have the OUTLET Disc Extra 1 but the program for Discovery won't work: all I get is B int- eger out of range, 1000:1,1. I have only just found this out with not having an Opus Discov- ery disk drive; I have never had occasion to use it. Can you please help me to get it to work? W.A. Yates

Brian Cavers to Arnold Yates

We do have software to read Opus on +D and visa versa but it is for double-density drives only and we have had no success with it at all.

You do not name the program on Extra 1 but I guess you mean TRANSBACK. I believe you have the +D version of Extra 1 and are loading TRANSBACK on your +D system which gives the error you report. TRANSBACK must be run on your Opus system to save Opus software to tape. You can then use UNITRANS+ (OUTLET 20) on the +D to load it from tape to +D disk. To transfer TRANSBACK to your Opus do the following...

1. You need a tape cassette recorder connected to the Spectrum using the +D. If you have a +2 then the one that is built in is fine but you will need another cassette machine attached to your Opus system. 2. If you have a 128K then switch to 48K mode. 3. Load TRANSBACK from +D. 4. Press BREAK. 5. Press R and the word RUN should appear. 6. Type 9983 7. Press ENTER and the prompt to save to tape should show. 8. Start the tape recording and press a key. 9. Load the program from the tape into your Opus system.

10.Ensure you have a disk with some room in your Opus drive. 10.Press BREAK on your Opus system. 11.Type RUN 9982. 12.Press ENTER 13.TRANSBACK should save to Opus disk.

You can now use TRANSBACK to get software from Opus to tape and then use UNITRANS+ on the +D to get it from tape to +D disk.

Brian

From Peter Johnson,NEW ZEALAND

Dear Brian and Ron,

This my second letter since joining. At the time of writing I have received and attempted to assimilate the contents of the first few copies of OUTLET.

I am very impressed with the range and variety of the material presented.It must be a difficult problem to maintain a balance so that the various interest areas are satisfied. You seem to be able to achieve this.

I was particularly interested in the description of the extens- ions to the SPECTRUM covered in Issue 80 by Rick Schuitemaker and also congratulate him on his efforts.

I must admit that I had been thinking along similar lines but on a much more modest scale:that of utilizing the unused capacity of the 48K extension memory if full-specification IC's are used.

By way of explanation for new- comers, when the SPECTRUM was extended to 48K [from the orig- inal 16K - Ed], the extra memory IC's used were not full specifi- cation types; they had some defects.

The IC's were apparently sorted into groups with useable upper or lower sections, half the IC was still functional and fitted to the Spectrum. There is a wire link on the circuit board to select which group of IC's were used.

If full specification IC's are used there is a further 32K of memory available. To use this requires some additional hard- ware in the form of two or three extra IC's to be fitted some- where to do the switching as with other larger memory vers- ions of the SPECTRUM. It is so obvious that I am sure that this must have been done before but I have seen nothing published.)

Back to the extensions by Rick: I am interested in doing this extension work to at least one of my 48K Spectrums. Although I have the facilities to design and produce the circuit boards there is no point in duplicating the effort if boards are avail- able.

In addition, mention was made of extra ROMs containing the additional functions to make use of the extensions. May I ask through these letters if the ROMs and circuit board are, or could be made,available? The ROM is most essential to fully explore the potential of this development.

I make no secret that my inter- est is in the more technical area and I would expect some criticism that the emphasis could be shifting in the content of OUTLET.My opinion is that the two interests are complimentry: without hardware there would be no need for software and visa versa.For the SPECTRUM to conti- nue it is necessary for it to be further developed and extended; its good features enhanced and it limitations minimised.

I have started to prepare a"wish list" of items where I think further development can be done. This I may forward to OUTLET in due course. I can contribute to the hardware side but am still a learner in software.

If we all attempt to understand something of what is published, be it in software or hardware, there is a further advance in our understanding of the Spec- trum.

In my original letter published in OUTLET 81, I mentioned my other interest in amateur radio and that I used a Spectrum as a terminal for the amateur radio packet system (as a reminder, packet radio is a worldwide system of linked bulletin boards using radio). What I did not mention was that I can be contacted by this means at address ZL4LV @ ZL4AA. ZL4lV is my amateur radio call sign and ZL4AA is the local bulletin board call sign.

The ZL stands for New Zealand. If any other OUTLET users use this system I would be interest- ed to hear from them. It should also be possible to transmit material for OUTLET by this means.

Peter Johnson.

Brian Cavers to Peter Johnson

There is no need to be defensive regarding topics of a technical or hardware side of computing! I for one am always delighted to receive and publish such items and am certain that many of our readers are too. I would be more than happy to have such articles in every single issue - to some extent that is what DRIVECHAT is intended to be, though it covers a wider miscellany of material.

I have been snowed under these last months, what with rewriting routines in the PC version and several days lost with 'flu but I shall strive to prepare your contributions for OUTLET soon!

They also supplied a 64K pack called SP80 which produced an 80K Spectrum with two pages of 32K which could be switched in at 32768 to 65535. Included with the RAM chips were three control chips and an LED.

The commands: OUT 65407,0 and OUT 49023,0 toggled between the two 32K pages of memory and the LED lit up for one but not the other to indicate which was in use. Of course, it was invisible inside the case in normal use!

I do not know if the SP80 used the same method you describe but it is of interest.

I often wonder why some company did not produce an extra 16K RAM to page in over the ROM so games could utilize the full 64K. Well of course the answer is that RAM was relatively expensive and it would be pretty useless without a significant number of games being made available. Possibly it might have been made useful to the BASIC programmer with a utility to copy the ROM into the new RAM but with some tiny extra routines overwritten unused or little used areas. Brian

Bill Clark, BARROW-IN-FURNESS

Dear Brian and Ron,

When using TYPELINER I can print out using all kinds of different print styles. Is it possible to do this using TASWORD which is what I'm using now. Also what is DATA MERGE for and how do you use it?

How do you alter TASWORD so that you can print 80 characters per line and print this out?

Do you know of any more secret messages on the +3 apart from the "HELLO, I'M A +3"? This also works on the  +2 but gives the same message as a +3.

I have an external +3 disk disk drive. When plugged in the back of my +3 I am given a report on the option screen which says Drives A: B: and M: available.

Unfortunately, all drives are disabled and nothing works until I disconnect my B: drive from the computer. I have tried various leads and different power packs but to no success.

With the B: drive plugged in I then go into +3 BASIC mode and type LOAD "B:". Then I insert a disk and type LOAD "filename". Nothing happens. The disk motor doesn't turn. It's as if the computer doesn't know the drive is there.

The same thing happens if I type LOAD "A:". If Drive B: is disconnected then the computer recognizes Drive A:. If B: is connected then the computer rec- ognizes nothing.

Please try and solve this for me as I've had all sorts of problems and blew up 5 different power packs which need repair- ing.

Best regards,

Bill Clark

Brian Cavers to Bill Clark

You don't say which version of Tasword you're using but I guess it's Tasword +3.

Tasword +3 of itself can't print out in different print styles.If you have a printer with variable fonts you can include printer codes in your document in the usual way, to change fonts and get double-height/double width, and so on if your printer has these features.

Tasword produced a separate pro- gram called TASPRINT PLUS THREE with 25 different fonts and a font designer, priced `24.95.It works with Tasword documents.

Unfortunately, like all Spectrum products,it is very difficult to find any supplier these days. It may be possible to get a copy at a computer fair or why not put in an advert in OUTBOARD or in MICROMART for a secondhand copy?

DATA MERGE lets you include a special character in your Tas- word document (the ampersand &) with a code letter. This acts as a marker. When you print the document using the "print with Data merge" feature, as well as the usual printer prompts, you are asked to enter a filename. As the document is printed the marker is replaced with text from this second file.

For example, you might have a standard letter you repeatedly send to people on request. You might normally load the letter into Tasword, type in the name and address of the person and any other details particular to the case and then print it. If instead you have a file full of names and addresses flagged as a data merge file you need only type the marker in the letter.It is obviously only of much use if you are printing multiple copies of a document.

The above example is known as "mail-merge" but it can be any text of course. In addition, you can merge in MASTERFILE +3 data saved with "data export".

Full details of DATA MERGE are given in the Tasword +3 manual starting at page 40.

To get 80 column...

1. Go to the main Tasword menu. 2. Press C to customise program. 3. Press ENTER to confirm. 4. Check TASWORD is in the drive 5. Press ENTER. 6. Press P to change the program 7. Press ENTER to confirm. 8. Press ENTER repeatedly until the flashing cursor goes down to "Right margin (64)" 9. Type 80. 10.Press ENTER repeatedly to end 11.Back at the custom menu. 12.Press EDIT for main menu. 13.Press R and ENTER for editor.

You should now be able to cursor right and when you reach the right side of the screen it will scroll left so you can go beyond 64 columns,in fact, to a maximum of 128 (even though 80 was put in! Bug?).

When you reach column 80 set the right margin in the usual way by pressing EXTEND to get extended mode then SYMBOL plus key "9" (right bracket) together.

Note: to make this permanent I think you need to resave TASWORD using the T option at the main menu. Otherwise, next time you load the program it will default to 64 columns again.

No, sorry, I don't know of any other hidden features or mess- ages of the +3 other than has been listed in OUTLET over rec- ent months. If you missed them then scan back over OUTLETTERS (see also John Garner's letter in this issue).

It sounds like your B drive is not connected right.Try MEEDMORE DISTRIBUTION on 051 521 2202. I believe they make up leads and are said to be helpful. See also James Castle's OUTLETTER with the address of a supplier who has "a lot of Sinclair leads".

If the cable is correctly wired then surely you must have some fault in the wiring of the B drive or in the +3 B drive out- put circuitry. Trouble is, I do not know of any computer repair company that will deal with +3 drive problems.

### От: Miles Kinloch, EDINBURGH

Дорогой Brian,

Старший байт системной переменной 23668/9 можно использовать как очень простой способ определения, в каком режиме находится Spectrum. Его не обмануть даже такими штуками, на которых спотыкаются некоторые проверки — например, `POKE 23611,205` (позволяющий печатать графические символы T и U).

Разница обусловлена тем, что таблица синтаксиса команд в 128K ROM находится в другом месте. Хотя младший байт меняется в зависимости от используемой команды, старший байт в рамках одного режима всегда должен оставаться неизменным. Попробуйте, например, следующее:

```basic
10 IF PEEK 23669=26 THEN PRINT "You're in 48K mode": GOTO 30
20 PRINT "You are in 128K mode": REM (независимо от модели машины)
30 STOP
```

По иронии судьбы, в руководстве к Спекки эта системная переменная описана как «крайне маловероятно полезная»!

Я сам натерпелся от зависаний из-за холодильника, чайника, выключателей света и прочих бытовых приборов по всему дому, хотя сетевое напряжение в нашем районе вполне стабильное. `POKE @11`. У этой переменной есть одна особенность. Если при загрузке (BOOT) настроить +D на использование собственного порта принтера, она перезаписывает процедуру печати в Spectrum своим собственным кодом.

Если же при загрузке настроить использование принтера Spectrum, то стандартная процедура остается нетронутой. Впоследствии туда можно записать `0`, чтобы +D модифицировал процедуру печати под свой порт.

Однако, если загрузиться со значением `0`, это напрямую затирает процедуру Спектрума, и последующий `POKE` со значением `1` уже не сможет восстановить исходную процедуру.

Вам придется записать в переменную `1`, заново сохранить DOS, сбросить Spectrum и перезагрузиться, чтобы переключиться с принтера +D на принтер Spectrum. Указание в руководстве на то, что его можно «включать и выключать», несколько вводит в заблуждение.

Мои Disciple и +D ведут себя именно так, как описано. О каком-либо исправлении мне неизвестно. Впрочем, поскольку я использую буферы данных между компьютером и принтером, Spectrum может выполнять команду `LPRINT` независимо от состояния принтера.

Разница между +D и Disciple в реакции на полное отсутствие подключенного принтера кроется в аппаратных различиях. Disciple требует от принтера оба логических сигнала — как высокий (HIGH / busy), так и низкий (LOW / ready), чтобы определить возможность отправки данных. Если сигнала нет вовсе (т.е. нет принтера), он по умолчанию переходит в состояние «готов к отправке». (Полагаю, это касается всех Disciple).

Интерфейсу +D для отправки данных требуется только один логический уровень от принтера (низкий). Состояния «OFF LINE» и «НЕТ ПРИНТЕРА» для +D эквивалентны и воспринимаются как условие, запрещающее передачу данных.

У обоих этих решений есть свои плюсы и минусы.

Можно добавить к +D, скажем, кнопку, которая при нажатии переводит соответствующую линию управления в нужный логический уровень, когда принтер не подключён. Это обманет +D, заставив его думать, что принтер на связи, и позволит выполнить команду LPRINT (разумеется, данные для печати будут потеряны).

Другой вариант — разработать «логическую коробочку» между компьютером и принтером, которая будет определять отсутствие принтера и выдавать на +D нужный сигнал управления, чтобы тот вел себя как Disciple — если «отсутствие принтера» действительно представляет проблему.

Кстати, о принтерах: возможно, вам будет интересно узнать, что существуют устройства для сопряжения последовательного вывода с параллельными принтерами или параллельного вывода с последовательными.

Проверка информационных кабелей визуальным осмотром (даже с лупой) может не выявить проблему: провод может казаться плотно зажатым в разъеме, но при этом не иметь надежного контакта.

Учитывая довольно «топорный» метод, при котором контакт разъема прорезает изоляцию ленточного шлейфа до проводников при сдавливании половинок корпуса: прозвонка между каждым выводом разъемов на обоих концах с шевелением кабеля может быть делом долгим, но необходимым для обнаружения проблемы.

Блоки питания для дисководов — это отдельная тема. Во-первых, существует два основных типа: требующие 12В и 5В. Однако более поздним моделям нужны только 5В. Разные дисководы, с которыми я сталкивался, различаются по потребляемому току, но в целом могут забирать до 500 мА, причем шаговый двигатель — самый прожорливый.

Кстати, мысль вслух: а какое сетевое напряжение в Малави? Здешние БП, вероятно, рассчитаны на 240В. Является ли местным стандартом 220В? Даже если на БП указано 220/240В, вполне может оказаться, что он рассчитан впритык для работы в нашей стране при 240В. Это вполне могло бы объяснить, почему БП на 350 мА не захотел работать там, хотя здесь с ним всё в порядке. Дело не столько в токе, сколько в номинальном напряжении. У меня были проблемы с дисководом MGT со встроенным БП. Хотя запас трансформатора по току намного превышал требуемый, его номинальное напряжение было слишком низким: его едва хватало для работы в идеальных условиях.

Между прочим, измерение тока, потребляемого дисководом, может вводить в заблуждение из-за импульсного характера работы шагового двигателя. Во время теста головка должна перемещаться взад-вперед между дорожками T0 и T79.

Я не понимаю, почему БП признали «неремонтопригодным». Возможно, его ремонт был экономически нецелесообразен, поскольку стоимость работы намного превышает цену новой детали. Если только проблема не кроется, скажем, в каком-то странном типе компонента или разъема, который сейчас невозможно достать. В конце концов, стабилизированный БП на 5В содержит относительно мало деталей, и все они легкодоступны (во всяком случае, у нас).

Трансформатор, конденсатор и 5-вольтовый стабилизатор — вот и всё, из чего состоят мои самодельные БП для дисководов. Я бы не рекомендовал обычные БП-вилки, которые продаются в магазинах. Они должны быть хорошо стабилизированы и иметь отличное сглаживание пульсаций (если только дисководы не относятся к типу, где 5-вольтовый стабилизатор стоит внутри корпуса самого привода, а внешний БП, соответственно, нестабилизированный).

Если подключить вольтметр к шине 5В на самом дисководе, и напряжение значительно превышает 5.25В и/или падает ниже 4.75В при работающем приводе (когда головка перемещается по дорожкам), то под подозрение попадает именно БП.

Боюсь, ничего из этого не дает конкретных ответов, но, возможно, поможет направить мысли в нужное русло.

Функция DATA MERGE позволяет вставлять в документ Tasword специальный символ (амперсанд `&`) с буквенным кодом, который служит маркером-меткой. Когда вы отправляете документ на печать с опцией «Print with Data merge», помимо обычных принтерных запросов программа попросит вас указать имя файла. В процессе печати этот маркер будет автоматически заменяться текстом из указанного второго файла.

К примеру, у вас может быть стандартное письмо, которое вы регулярно рассылаете разным людям по запросу. В обычном случае вам пришлось бы загружать письмо в Tasword, каждый раз вручную впечатывать имя, адрес и другие уникальные детали, а затем отправлять на печать. Если же вместо этого у вас есть файл со списком имен и адресов, размеченный как файл для слияния данных (data merge), достаточно лишь расставить маркеры в тексте письма. Очевидно, что эта функция по-настоящему полезна только при печати множества персонализированных копий одного документа.

Этот прием широко известен как «mail-merge» (слияние почты), но подставляемым текстом, разумеется, может быть все что угодно. Кроме того, можно подтягивать данные из MASTERFILE +3, сохраненные через «data export».

Подробное описание работы DATA MERGE приведено в руководстве пользователя Tasword +3, начиная со страницы 40.

Чтобы включить режим 80 колонок:

1. Выйдите в главное меню Tasword.
2. Нажмите `C`, чтобы перейти к настройке программы (customise).
3. Нажмите `ENTER` для подтверждения.
4. Убедитесь, что диск с TASWORD находится в приводе.
5. Нажмите `ENTER`.
6. Нажмите `P` для изменения параметров программы.
7. Нажмите `ENTER` для подтверждения.
8. Нажимайте `ENTER` до тех пор, пока мигающий курсор не опустится на строку «Right margin (64)».
9. Введите `80`.
10. Нажимайте `ENTER` до самого конца списка опций.
11. Вы вернетесь в меню настроек.
12. Нажмите `EDIT` для выхода в главное меню.
13. Нажмите `R` и `ENTER` для перехода в редактор.

Теперь вы сможете перемещать курсор вправо, и по достижении правой границы экрана он начнет прокручиваться влево, позволяя выйти за пределы 64 колонок — фактически вплоть до максимума в 128 (хотя мы задавали 80! Баг?).

Дойдя до 80-й колонки, установите правую границу обычным способом: нажмите `EXTEND` для перехода в расширенный режим, а затем одновременно `SYMBOL SHIFT` и клавишу «9» (правая скобка).

Примечание: чтобы сохранить эти изменения навсегда, вам, скорее всего, нужно пересохранить TASWORD, используя опцию T в главном меню. Иначе при следующей загрузке программы она снова по умолчанию перейдет в 64 колонки.
